problem: The rows are written MSB-first, so the leftmost cell of 10100101 is bit 7. But the figure is drawn with show_index and index_from 0, so the columns are labelled 0 to 7 from the left. The label '4' therefore sits under a cell that is really bit 3, and the label '2' under a cell that is really bit 5. A student reading the index labels concludes bit 0 is the leftmost bit, which is exactly what the exam trap warns against.
fix: Either reverse every row so the cells run LSB-first (bit 0 at index 0): PORT1 ['1','0','1','0','0','1','0','1'] becomes ['1','0','1','0','0','1','0','1'] reversed = ['1','0','1','0','0','1','0','1'] — write it as 1010 0101 with bit 0 on the left and move the marks to index 3 and index 5; or keep MSB-left and drop the numeric index labels so no bit numbers are printed, listing the bit numbers 7…0 separately.

problem: The sentence 'For bit n, 1  has a single 1 at position n' has a missing shift expression, so the sentence as printed is false (the number 1 has its only 1 at position 0).
fix: For bit n, (1 << n) has a single 1 at position n and 0 everywhere else.

where: Exam traps, second bullet, and Quiz Q6
problem: Both write 'p |= 0x08 & 0x20', but everywhere else p is the pointer (volatile uint8_t *p) and the register is *p. As written, p |= ... increments the pointer, not the port.
fix: *p |= 0x08 & 0x20 is wrong; use *p |= (0x08 | 0x20) to set the two bits.

problem: 'Both do read-modify-write' is not accurate for 8051 sbit access. Writing an sbit such as LED = 1 compiles to a single-bit instruction (SETB/CLR) on the bit-addressable port latch; it is not a read-modify-write of the whole byte. Read-modify-write happens only when C writes the whole port, as in P1 |= 0x08.
fix: Say: writing the whole byte P1 |= 0x08 is a read-modify-write; writing a single sbit uses an atomic bit instruction. On ARM the pointer write is a read-modify-write of the register.

problem: The lead says Embedded C 'adds fixed-width integer types'. The types uint8_t, int16_t and uint32_t are standard C (C99, <stdint.h>), not an embedded extension; what embedded code adds is their use for register layouts plus volatile, masks and ISR syntax.
fix: Embedded C keeps C syntax and relies on the standard fixed-width types from <stdint.h>, together with volatile register accesses, bit masks and interrupt functions.
